rationale: B wins because its proof asks and reporter shapes are sharper. It turns the free rollout into a real sustainability story — "Here's who's actually paying" — while A reaches for the lazier market jab, "while rivals still charge for it," before proving the rivals or the pricing. B still invents a few bridges, but it gives a founder cleaner reporting assignments.
gaps_in_A: "while rivals still charge for it" asserts competitor pricing the update does not provide. If the proof list says you still need comparable pricing, it cannot sit in the headline as fact.
"paid commercial products versus a large donor-funded free entrant" decorates a real nonprofit/free fact into a market split that has not been established.
"which tends to center on students" invents a prior-coverage pattern. That may be true, but it is not in the update.
"Free AI lesson-planning help arrives for teachers already stretched thin" leans on a generic teacher-burnout trope without workload data, time-saved proof, or named teachers.
gaps_in_B: "districts are signing on to expand to 1 million students based on a study" invents causality. The update says the rollout and results are arriving together, not that districts relied on the study.
"While VC-backed EdTech companies charge districts" asserts competitor business models and pricing without proof from the update.
"a body of research on productive failure and desirable difficulty argues" imports outside research as an established peg. Fine as a proof target, not fine as a supplied fact.
"journalist-fit-check" is premature as the next step. Close the methodology, donor, and teacher-source holes before matching reporters to half-built angles.
